items.stimulus:
A marine biologist measures the shell length of a juvenile green sea turtle in a rehabilitation tank once a week.

| Week | Shell length (cm) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 12.0 |
| 1 | 13.5 |
| 2 | 15.0 |

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the shell length of the turtle changes over time?
items.explanation: The length goes up each week, so it is increasing. The differences are all the same: 13.5 − 12.0 = 1.5, 15.0 − 13.5 = 1.5, 16.5 − 15.0 = 1.5. A constant amount added each step means the relationship is linear, so it is increasing linear.

B.why: You saw a constant difference, so linear is right, but you flipped the direction. The lengths get larger each week, so the relationship is increasing.

D.why: Both the direction and the type are wrong. The lengths rise, and they rise by the same amount each week, so this is increasing linear, not decreasing exponential.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how the amplitude of the string's vibration changes over time?

items.subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing
items.stimulus: Two folklore archives are digitizing recorded oral tales. Archive A started with 360 digitized tales and adds 90 tales at the end of each year. Archive B started with 40 digitized tales, and at the end of each year its total grows by 100%. The number of tales in each archive $t$ years after digitizing began is modeled by $A(t) = 360 + 90t$ and $B(t) = 40(2)^t$.
items.stem: Which of the following statements about the two collections is true for whole-number values of $t$?
choices: Archive A has more tales than Archive B for every value of $t$.
Archive B first has more tales than Archive A when $t = 3$.
Archive B first has more tales than Archive A when $t = 4$.
Archive B first has more tales than Archive A when $t = 5$.
items.explanation: Exponential growth always overtakes linear growth eventually, so test values until it happens. When $t = 4$, $A(4) = 360 + 360 = 720$ and $B(4) = 40(16) = 640$, so A is still ahead. When $t = 5$, $A(5) = 810$ and $B(5) = 40(32) = 1{,}280$. Archive B first has more tales when $t = 5$.

A.why: This is the comparison trap. You looked at the first few years, when A is far ahead (450 tales to 80 when $t = 1$), and assumed that would last. B doubles every year, and doubling eventually overtakes any fixed yearly addition.

B.why: When $t = 3$, B's yearly increase (160 tales) first exceeds A's increase of 90, so B is growing faster from then on. But B's total is still only 320 against A's 630. You compared the yearly additions instead of the totals.

C.why: You were off by one year when you evaluated A and used $360 + 90(3) = 630$ for $t = 4$, which made B's 640 look larger. The correct value is $A(4) = 720$, which is still larger than 640.

items.stimulus: In year 0, weaving workshop A produced 600 meters of cloth and workshop B produced 300 meters. Each year after that, A's output increased by 20% of its year-0 output. B's output increased by 25% of the previous year's output.
items.stem: What is the least whole number of years $n$ after year 0 for which workshop B's output is greater than workshop A's output?
items.explanation: A adds 20% of a fixed amount, which is 120 m every year, so it is linear: $A(n) = 600 + 120n$. B is exponential: $B(n) = 300(1.25)^n$. In year 7, $A = 1{,}440$ and $B \approx 1{,}430.5$, so A is still ahead. In year 8, $A = 1{,}560$ and $B \approx 1{,}788.1$. The answer is year 8.

D.why: You treated A's 20% increase as compounding, $600(1.2)^n$. But A grows by 20% of its year-0 output, a fixed 120 m each year, so A is linear. Compared with that linear A, B pulls ahead much sooner.

items.stimulus: Two archaeological collections of unglazed pottery are deteriorating. Collection P starts with 600 intact pieces and loses 30 pieces each decade until none remain. items.stem: Which statement correctly compares the two collections for whole numbers of decades $n$ from 0 to 25?
choices: Q has more pieces than P in every decade from 0 through 25.
Q has fewer pieces than P in every decade from 3 through 25.
Q has fewer pieces than P in every decade from 3 through 20 only.
Q has fewer pieces than P in every decade from 3 through 19 only.
items.explanation: $P(n) = 600 - 30n$ until it reaches 0 at $n = 20$, and $Q(n) = 900(0.8)^n$. At $n = 2$, $Q = 576 > 540$. C.why: You found that P reaches 0 at $n = 20$ and stopped the interval there. In decade 20 itself, P has 0 pieces and Q has about 10, so Q is already ahead in that decade.

items.stimulus: In a pest-control trial, the number of aphids on a test plot $w$ weeks after the trial begins is modeled by $a(w) = 5(2)^w$, and the number of ladybugs released on the plot is modeled by $\ell(w) = 500 + 60w$.
items.stem: What is the least whole number of weeks $w$ for which $a(w) > \ell(w)$?
items.explanation: Test whole values. At $w = 7$, $a = 640$ and $\ell = 920$. At $w = 8$, $a = 1{,}280$ and $\ell = 980$. So the aphids first outnumber the ladybugs in week 8. You can also graph both functions in Desmos and find where they intersect, between 7 and 8.

A.why: You compared only the first weeks. The ladybugs start at 500 and gain 60 a week, while the aphids gain only 5 in week 1. But exponential growth always passes linear growth eventually.

D.why: You divided both sides by 5 but divided only the 500. That gave $2^w > 100 + 60w$ instead of $2^w > 100 + 12w$, which pushed the crossover too late.
